title: Opioid intoxication: hypothermia, hypotension, decreased tidal volume
vignette: A 26-year-old man with depressed mental status is brought to the emergency department by police. Due to fear of arrest, he swallowed a handful of pills as the officers approached him. On examination, the patient responds to painful stimuli but is somnolent. Pupils are <2 mm. Respirations are 6/min. Lungs are clear to auscultation. Which of the following additional findings (temperature, blood pressure, tidal volume) are most likely present in this patient?

clues.note: An acute ingestion presenting with CNS depression frames this as a toxidrome to identify from the exam. (Sensitive presentation - handled as clinical toxicology.)
Pinpoint pupils (miosis) with depressed consciousness are a hallmark of OPIOID intoxication.
Bradypnea (respiratory depression) is the most dangerous and characteristic feature of opioid overdose.

whatMatters: Somnolence + MIOSIS (pinpoint pupils) + RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION = OPIOID intoxication (classic triad). Additional expected findings: HYPOTHERMIA (impaired thermogenesis), HYPOTENSION (histamine-mediated vasodilation), and DECREASED TIDAL VOLUME (reduced ventilatory drive). Answer F (all three decreased). Reverse with naloxone.
strategy: Recognize the opioid toxidrome (CNS depression + miosis + hypoventilation), then predict its autonomic/respiratory profile: temperature DOWN, blood pressure DOWN (mildly), tidal volume DOWN (with the low respiratory rate). Pick the row with all three decreased. Reject rows showing increases (those fit sympathomimetic/anticholinergic toxidromes, not opioids).

eliminations.label: All increased - sympathomimetic, not opioid
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: elevated temperature/BP with increased ventilation. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: that fits a sympathomimetic (cocaine/amphetamine) toxidrome; opioids DEPRESS these. ✅ Correct if: stimulant intoxication (hyperthermia, hypertension, tachypnea).

eliminations.label: ↑temp/↑BP with ↓tidal volume - mixed/incorrect
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: raised temperature/BP but low tidal volume. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: opioids lower temperature and BP too; this partial pattern doesn't fit. ✅ Correct if: a different combined toxidrome, not opioids.

eliminations.label: ↑temp/↓BP/↑tidal volume - inconsistent
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: hyperthermia with hypotension and increased ventilation. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: opioids cause hypoVENTILATION (low tidal volume) and hypoTHERMIA, not this mix. ✅ Correct if: sepsis/other, not opioid overdose.

eliminations.label: ↓temp/↑BP/↓tidal volume - BP is wrong direction
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: hypothermia and low tidal volume but HIGH BP. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: opioids tend to LOWER blood pressure (histamine-mediated vasodilation), not raise it. ✅ Correct if: hypothermia with a pressor effect (not opioids).

eliminations.label: All increased - duplicate sympathomimetic pattern
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: everything up. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: same as A - opposite of the opioid (depressant) toxidrome. ✅ Correct if: stimulant intoxication.

reasoning: Somnolence + pinpoint pupils + respiratory depression = opioid intoxication (classic triad)
Opioids depress thermoregulation and ventilation and cause histamine-mediated vasodilation
So temperature, blood pressure, and tidal volume all decrease
mechanism: Opioids act on mu (and kappa/delta) receptors throughout the CNS, spinal cord, and GI tract. The classic acute intoxication TRIAD is DECREASED RESPIRATORY RATE, MIOSIS (pinpoint pupils), and DEPRESSED MENTAL STATUS; respiratory depression is the most lethal effect and the best predictor of overdose. Additional findings all reflect CNS/autonomic depression: HYPOTHERMIA (opioid effects on central thermoregulation plus reduced ability to respond to the environment), HYPOTENSION (usually mild; opioids trigger histamine release from mast cells causing vasodilation), and DECREASED TIDAL VOLUME (brainstem respiratory-center depression reduces both rate AND depth of breathing, blunting the response to hypercapnia/hypoxia). GI effects (decreased motility -> constipation) are also common. Thus temperature, blood pressure, and tidal volume are all decreased. The antidote is NALOXONE (a competitive mu-opioid antagonist). Increases in these parameters would instead suggest a sympathomimetic toxidrome. (Sensitive topic: if you or someone you know is struggling, contacting a clinician or crisis line is appropriate - I can help find resources.)

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Pharm/Tox > opioid toxidrome: respiratory depression + miosis + CNS depression; also hypothermia, hypotension, ↓tidal volume, constipation; reverse with naloxone.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Opioids depress everything: temperature, BP, and tidal volume all fall.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on toxidrome, miosis, tidal volume, respiratory depression, or naloxone? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Increases in temperature/BP/ventilation fit a SYMPATHOMIMETIC toxidrome, not opioids.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: opioid triad = ↓RR + miosis + ↓mental status; also ↓temp, ↓BP, ↓tidal volume; antidote naloxone. Sensitive topic - resources available.

firstAid.detail: Tox > sympathomimetic (all up) vs opioid (all down).
Pharm > competitive mu-opioid antagonist reverses respiratory depression.

memoryHook: Opioids are the great depressant: pupils pinpoint, breaths shallow and slow, and temperature and blood pressure all sag - naloxone flips the switch back on.
